title: Numbers and age
goal: Count to a thousand, say your age and birthday, and accept the fact that in Finnish, numbers make the noun change its form.
bekal: build the numbers 0–1,000 out of just ten pieces
use the partitive after numbers: *kaksi kirja**a***, not *kaksi kirjat*
give your age, date of birth, and phone number

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ilmoittautuminen
dialogs.intro: Budi is signing up for the next-level course. Sanna, the office clerk, fills in the form as she asks questions.

lines.speaker: Sanna:
lines.text: Hyvää päivää! Mikä sinun koko nimesi on?
lines.id: Good afternoon! What's your full name?
lines.literal: good day! what your whole name-your is?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Budi Santoso. Anteeksi, voitko toistaa hitaammin?
lines.id: Budi Santoso. Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly?
lines.literal: Budi Santoso. sorry, can-?-you repeat more-slowly?

lines.speaker: Sanna:
lines.text: Totta kai. Kuinka vanha sinä olet?

lines.literal: true of-course. how old you are?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nolla neljä nolla, kaksi kuusi kolme, seitsemän yksi yhdeksän.
lines.id: Zero four zero, two six three, seven one nine.
lines.literal: zero four zero, two six three, seven one nine.

lines.speaker: Sanna:
lines.text: Kiitos. Kuinka monta kieltä sinä puhut?

lines.id: Three languages well and one badly — Finnish!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good. How many students are in a group?

lines.speaker: Sanna:
lines.id: Nine or ten. Welcome to the course!

notes: **After a number, the noun is partitive and SINGULAR.** *Kaksitoista viikko**a*** — not *viikot*. This truly goes against instinct: twelve weeks, but the word is singular. It makes sense from the inside: the number already states the quantity, so the noun only names "what kind of thing" — a bit like English "a twelve-week course" or "ten head of cattle", where the noun doesn't go plural either.
**Except after yksi.** *Yksi kirja* uses the basic form, because one item is a whole item. From *kaksi* on, everything is partitive.
**Vuotta, not vuosia.** *Vuosi* (year) becomes *vuotta* in the partitive — one of the most irregular forms you'll use often. Its cousins: *kuukausi → kuukautta* (month), *uusi → uutta* (new).

**Kuinka monta and montako mean the same thing.** Both mean "how many", and both require the partitive singular after them: *kuinka monta kiel**tä***, *montako opiskelija**a***. *Montako* is shorter and heard more often.
**Phone numbers are read digit by digit.** No combining digits as English sometimes does ("double four"). Zero is always *nolla*, never the letter "o".

**Kolmastoista maaliskuuta** uses two forms at once: an ordinal number (*kolmastoista* = thirteenth) and the month name in the partitive (*maaliskuu → maaliskuuta*). This pattern is the same for every date, so memorize the shape now; ordinal numbers are covered in Unit 16.

grammars.title: Numbers 0–1,000
body: Ten basic numbers plus two pieces (*-toista* and *-kymmentä*) are enough to build everything up to a hundred. Note that Finnish numbers are written **as one word**, however long they get.
after: **-toista** literally means "of the second" — that is, "so-many of the second ten". So *kolmetoista* = "three of the second ten" = 13. It does the job of English "-teen", but it carries a real meaning.

⚠️ **8 and 9 are built by subtraction.** *Kahdeksan* and *yhdeksän* contain *kaksi* and *yksi* — originally "two short (of ten)" and "one short". That's history, not a rule you need to apply, but it helps you remember the long forms.
The tens use *-kymmentä*, which is actually the partitive of *kymmenen* — so *kolmekymmentä* literally means "three of ten". The numbers themselves obey the partitive-after-numbers rule.

grammars.title: Number + partitive singular
body: The rule in one sentence: **after numbers from two up, the noun is partitive and stays singular.** What needs practice is forming the partitive.
after: The pattern: words ending in a **single vowel** simply double that last vowel (*kirja → kirjaa*). Words ending in *-i*, *-si*, or *-nen* take the ending **-ta/-tä** and often change their stem (*kieli → kieltä*, *ihminen → ihmistä*).
⚠️ *Lapsi → lasta* and *vuosi → vuotta* can't be guessed from the basic form. Such words are few but very frequent, so memorize the partitive together with the word itself.
The same rule applies after *paljon* (much, a lot), *vähän* (a little), *monta* (many, countable), and *kuinka monta / montako* (how many).

blocks.text: Both ways of giving your age are correct. *Olen 26* is shortest and most common; *Olen 26-vuotias* ("I'm a 26-year-old") is a bit fuller and is required when the age becomes an adjective: *26-vuotias mies* (a 26-year-old man).

Every month name ends in *-kuu*, which means "moon" — the moon in the sky and the month on the calendar are the same word, just as "month" and "moon" share a root in English. The first part comes from what happens in nature that month: *heinäkuu* = hay month, *lokakuu* = mud month, *joulukuu* = Christmas month.

blocks.title: Two numbers that are easy to mix up
items: **kuusi** = six, but *kuusi* also means **spruce tree**. Two identical words; only the context tells them apart. *Kuusi kuusta* = six spruce trees.
**seitsemän** and **kahdeksan** are both long and often get mixed up by ear. A handle: *seitsemän* has an *s* up front, like "seven" and German "sieben"; *kahdeksan* contains the *kah-* from *kaksi*.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Decimal commas and thousands work the other way around from English. Finland uses a comma for decimals (*3,5* is read *kolme pilkku viisi*, "three comma five") and a space for thousands (*10 000*). So the English 1,000.50 is written *1 000,50* in Finland.
